sections.body: Artificial intelligence in medicine is the use of pattern recognition and prediction software on clinical data, from scans and genomes to notes and vital signs. In practice it is already doing narrow, well defined jobs: flagging suspected strokes on head scans, drafting visit notes from recorded conversation, ranking drug candidates before any wet lab work begins, and watching intensive care monitors for early signs of deterioration. These systems do not diagnose on their own. They sort, score and prioritise, and a clinician remains responsible for the decision. The work spans hospitals, imaging centres, laboratories and public health agencies, and it touches both the bedside and the back office. What unites the ten areas here is that each turns messy biological or operational data into something a person can act on faster.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some areas are further along than others. Imaging has the most mature evidence base, with systems cleared for specific tasks such as detecting certain findings in mammography or retinal scans, though performance often drops when a model meets a new hospital's equipment and patient mix. Documentation tools have spread quickly because the benefit is easy to feel, but accuracy on accents, drug names and overlapping speech is uneven. Genomics and drug discovery remain mostly research stage, where a promising molecule or target still needs years of trials. Intensive care prediction, triage and population health raise harder questions about bias, alert fatigue and who acts on a warning at three in the morning. Regulation is catching up slowly, and security of connected devices is a known weak point. The honest limit across all ten is that few systems have been tested in randomised trials showing that patients actually do better, and that is the standard that matters.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from the body outward to the system. Diagnostic Imaging and Radiology and Genomic Medicine and Precision Therapeutics cover reading and interpreting biological signals, one visual and one molecular. Clinical Documentation and Ambient Intelligence and Surgical Robotics and Navigation sit closer to the encounter itself, one handling the record and one handling the operating room. Predictive Patient Analytics and Intensive Care and Drug Discovery and Molecular Simulation look forward in time, at deterioration and at candidate molecules. Telemedicine and Triage and Epidemiology and Population Health widen the frame to remote care and to whole populations. Neuroinformatics and the Brain stands somewhat apart, dealing with the organ that is both the subject and the metaphor. Governance, Compliance and Medical Device Security closes the section because every page before it depends on devices that are approved, monitored and defended. A reader new to the field can start with imaging or documentation for concrete examples, then move to governance to understand why deployment is slower than the demonstrations suggest.
